transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-18
Time: 15:32 UTC
Duration: ~52 mins
Attendees: Alex Morales (Redwood AE), Sofia Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Catalyst), Liam O'Connor (Catalyst), Jordan Reed (Catalyst), Rina Kapoor (Redwood CSM)

[00:00] Alex Morales: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, im alex from redwood, that's sofia our se, rina on cs. ready to dive into latency and throughput needs.
[00:23] Maya Patel: thanks alex. quick context: we're Catalyst Retail, ML team supporting real-time personalization for checkout and search. main ask: we need p95 under 120ms for short prompts (~40 tokens) at 200 concurrent sessions, streaming enabled for partial responses.
[00:45] Sofia Chen: ok got it. When you say 200 concurrent sessions, is that steady-state or bursts? and what's your token/sec per session roughly?
[01:02] Liam O'Connor: mostly steady during peak windows, bursts up to 400 concurrent. token/sec per session around 15-20 when streaming; avg prompt length 35-60 input tokens + about 40 output tokens.
[01:22] Jordan Reed: security is big for us - we need SOC2, SSO (SAML), KMS integration for keys, and option for VPC/private deployment for production.
[01:38] Alex Morales: great. high level: Redwood supports Hosted API, Dedicated reserved capacity and Private (VPC/on-prem). for p95 120ms on short requests, Hosted might work with our high-performance runtime but Dedicated gives more predictable tail latency since you get pinned GPU pools. Private gives full network control for compliance but you might manage hardware variability.
[02:05] Sofia Chen: some quick clarifying Qs: are you streaming token-by-token to the client or using chunked partial responses? how tolerant is the client to variable first-byte times?
[02:20] Maya Patel: we stream token-by-token into our UI; first byte latency is important for perceived responsiveness. p95 matter more than median.
[02:32] Sofia Chen: ok. for streaming the runtime maintains KV cache and incremental decoding; note our infra optimizes for short sequences and can route requests to low-latency hosts. small caveat - sometimes transcription shows KV 'cash' in our logs, heh, the SE jokes.
[02:52] Liam O'Connor: haha. real talk - what's typical tokens/sec throughput per GPU? we've seen docs quoting 1k-3k tokens/sec depending on model and quantization.
[03:08] Sofia Chen: yeah that range is common; example: on a 16-bit fp16 bfloat setup for a 7b-style model you might see 1.5k tokens/sec single-stream, but with batching and continuous KV caching across sessions we can boost aggregate tokens/sec significantly. Dedicated lets you control batch windows and concurrency shaping.
[03:33] Jordan Reed: any guidance on p95 -> model sizing? we worry about occasionally long tails when models hit cold KV caches.
[03:44] Sofia Chen: p95 tail is often from cold starts, long context windows, or scheduling interference. our Dedicated offering pins capacity so you avoid co-tenancy interference. caching strategies (prefetch, prefix caching) reduce cold-starts; for your 40-token responses and 35-60 inputs, keeping kv warm with session pinning or sticky routing helps.
[04:05] Maya Patel: for the benchmark we want to reproduce realistic traffic: mix of short personalization prompts (70% < 60 tokens) and longer compositional requests (30% ~200 tokens), streaming enabled. also measure first-byte, last-byte, p50/p95/p99, and tokens/sec sustained over 1 hour.
[04:29] Sofia Chen: perfect - we can run a 1-hour token/sec benchmark on Hosted and Dedicated replica if you'd like. we'll instrument p95 metrics and push profiler traces. we'll need a sample dataset and workload profile from you.
[04:46] Liam O'Connor: sample dataset we can provide; also can we test with our VPC peering to simulate on-prem latency?
[04:55] Alex Morales: yes for Private or Dedicated in your cloud region we can peer. Hosted will be over internet but we run edge routing. for strict residency and control you'd use Private (VPC), but that's more setup.
[05:12] Jordan Reed: cost question - how does Dedicated compare to Hosted per token and for idle capacity?
[05:20] Alex Morales: Hosted is pay-as-you-go, so burst-friendly; Dedicated is committed monthly/annual with lower per-token costs at scale but you pay for reserved capacity. We'll send a side-by-side pricing sheet.
[05:33] Maya Patel: since latency is critical, what's your typical p95 for short prompts on Hosted in us-east?
[05:40] Sofia Chen: in us-east for our optimized 7b-like models, p95 for short prompts often falls in 80-140ms on Hosted depending on network path and exact prompt shape. with Dedicated we commonly hit 60-110ms p95 for same model due to isolation and busy-loop scheduling. note numbers can vary by model family and quantization.
[06:02] Liam O'Connor: about quantization - we use INT8 in some places; does Redwood runtimes support quantized kernels? any quality tradeoffs?
[06:10] Sofia Chen: yes we support quantized paths and select kernels optimized for int8/4-bit quant. we include model quality checks and you can opt for quantization profiles we recommend per workload. sometimes 4-bit introduces minor quality diffs for certain tasks; we recommend running evals on your prompt set as part of the pilot.
[06:32] Maya Patel: great. on security: you mentioned KMS integration - can we bring our own keys (BYOK) and HSM?
[06:40] Alex Morales: yes, Dedicated and Private support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations; Hosted also supports BYOK through our KMS integrations for encryption-at-rest. we'll attach SOC2+ISO docs and KMS integration notes in the follow-up.
[06:57] Jordan Reed: can you do SAML SSO for console and RBAC for developers?
[07:03] Rina Kapoor: yep, SAML SSO for console and fine-grained RBAC for routes and tokens. audit logs are shipped to customer SIEMs or stored per retention policy.
[07:16] Liam O'Connor: ok for the benchmark, what metrics do you capture out-of-the-box?
[07:22] Sofia Chen: we capture request/response times (first byte, last byte), per-token latency, token throughput, GPU utilization, queueing latency, KV cache hit rates, and sampling traces. We'll provide a dashboard link in the pilot.
[07:38] Maya Patel: perfect. to confirm success criteria: p95 < 120ms for short prompts at 200 steady concurrency with streaming enabled, less than 10% error/no-response, and tokens/sec sustained to meet peak RPS.
[07:55] Alex Morales: noted. we'd propose a 3-week pilot: week 1 setup + security review, week 2 benchmark w/ tuning, week 3 result review + canary plan. does that timeline work?
[08:08] Jordan Reed: yes sounds good; our infra team (liam) will lead the peering and SSO work.
[08:16] Liam O'Connor: one more technical nit: do you support sticky routing per session id to keep KV warm across subsequent calls?
[08:24] Sofia Chen: yes we support session affinity and can pin sessions to nodes for duration; we also have prefix caching to reuse KV across similar prompts.
[08:34] Maya Patel: how about fallback strategies if Dedicated capacity saturates during Black Friday style peaks?
[08:41] Alex Morales: we provide smart routing and failover: policy-based routing can fallback to a compatible Hosted pool or a lower-cost model variant. you can set automatic fallback policies so user-facing services stay online with graceful degradation.
[08:55] Jordan Reed: any pitfalls customers hit during bench runs?
[09:02] Sofia Chen: common ones: not simulating realistic client-side backpressure, using large batch windows that hurt tail latency, or not warming KV caches. we'll share a bench harness that includes backpressure patterns and jitter to simulate real sessions.
[09:18] Maya Patel: excellent. on dataset privacy: we'll want to redact PII before sending samples; is that ok for bench?
[09:24] Alex Morales: totally fine - redact or synthetic is common. we just need representative token distributions and prompt templates.
[09:31] Liam O'Connor: small follow-up: for streaming metrics, does your instrumentation break down per-token latency vs network transmission?
[09:38] Sofia Chen: yes we capture server-side token generation time and client-side network transmission when you attach our SDK or run the harness; we'll include both in the dashboard.
[09:50] Jordan Reed: let's talk SLAs - what's typical for Dedicated?
[09:56] Alex Morales: Dedicated comes with SLA for uptime and latency tiers depending on the commitment. we'll include SLA options in the pricing doc.
[10:05] Maya Patel: ok next steps recap?
[10:08] Alex Morales: recap: Alex to send pricing + model perf matrix + SOC2/ISO & KMS notes; Sofia to prepare benchmark harness and scripts; Catalyst to send sample datasets and expected SLOs; Liam to confirm VPC and SSO requirements; schedule 1-hour benchmark next Tue.
[10:26] Jordan Reed: sounds good. any blockers?
[10:29] Maya Patel: none from us. we'll aim to get datasets by Friday.
[10:33] Alex Morales: great - we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs. thanks all.
[10:38] (call ends)

Notes about transcript quality: auto-transcription had a few mis-hearings (KV cash, some names). action items are captured above.

Bench specifics discussed (for reference):
- Traffic profile: 70% short (<60 tokens) streaming personalization, 30% long (~200 tokens) composition requests
- Concurrency: steady 200, burst 400
- Success criteria: p95 < 120ms short prompts, <10% errors, sustain tokens/sec to meet peak RPS
- Bench runs to be executed on Hosted and Dedicated; Private considered later if peering shows network variability or compliance requires it

References mentioned: pricing spreadsheet (link to be sent), SOC2 + ISO attestation pack (link), benchmark harness repo (link)
